claims.text: Static EAM reference potentials inadequately represent the configurational diversity of ab initio liquids in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.

An actively learned ML interatomic potential trained on ab initio high-temperature liquid and solid configurations will capture chemically complex many-body environments better than a static EAM potential.
A moment tensor potential can model both random and short-range-ordered configurations in a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The ML potential should be continuously updated with ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations from the target alloy.
The trained ML potential should be used as the reference potential in TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration.
The proposed reference will sample local short-range order and a broad spectrum of atomic environments in disordered liquid and high-temperature solid states.
Local short-range order and other sampled atomic environments mediate free-energy contributions.
EAM potentials oversimplify bond-angle variability and local chemical ordering in these alloys.
Training on a broad ab initio configuration set will adjust the ML potential's energy landscape to represent the variability of local atomic environments.
Improved representation of local environments will increase phase-space overlap between the reference and ab initio free-energy surfaces.
Increased reference–target phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The method is applicable to refractory or transition-metal-based HEAs containing four to eight principal elements.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 0.9–1.0 times the alloy melting temperature.
The method should be most effective in alloys with more than four elements and strong local chemical fluctuations.
The ML reference may be less beneficial for low-melting alloys or alloys already well described by EAM.
Using the ML reference could reduce integration-path mismatch by approximately 50% relative to the EAM reference.
The ML-reference free energies will converge closer to direct ab initio free-energy benchmarks than EAM-reference results.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the quality of the ML training set and the complexity of the alloy.
The hypothesis is falsified if the ML reference improves path mismatch by less than approximately 20% relative to EAM.
The hypothesis is falsified if the ML-reference free energy does not improve agreement with the direct ab initio benchmark to better than approximately 20 meV per atom.
